lesson.title: The Matching Game: Telling f, f', and f'' Apart
lesson.summary: When three unlabeled graphs are shown together, each one is secretly the derivative of the one before it, and a short list of reliable checks, zero-slope-to-zero-crossing, symmetry type, and shape complexity, reveals which graph is which.
lesson.body:
A common exam and textbook exercise shows three graphs, labeled only A, B, and C, and asks which is f, which is f', and which is f''. Building f from f' and building f' from f already give the two core reading skills needed; connecting all three at once just means applying both skills simultaneously and using them to cross check each other.

Three tests are reliable enough to use every time. First, the zero-slope test: every horizontal tangent (peak, valley, or flat spot) on a candidate f graph must line up with a zero crossing on the candidate f' graph at that same x-value, and likewise every horizontal tangent on the f' graph must line up with a zero crossing on the f'' graph. Second, the symmetry test: differentiating an even function produces an odd function, and differentiating an odd function produces an even function, so if one graph is symmetric about the y-axis and another is symmetric about the origin, that is a strong hint about which one differentiates into which. Third, the complexity test: differentiating a polynomial lowers its degree by one, so among three polynomial-shaped graphs, the one with the most bends and turns generally sits earliest in the chain (as f), and the graphs get progressively simpler moving toward f''.

Let f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2 = x^2(x^2 - 2). This is even, since f(-x) = x^4 - 2x^2 = f(x), so its graph is symmetric about the y-axis. Its derivative is f'(x) = 4x^3 - 4x = 4x(x - 1)(x + 1), with roots at x = -1, 0, and 1; checking signs shows f' is negative on (-infinity, -1), positive on (-1, 0), negative on (0, 1), and positive on (1, infinity). That means f has a local minimum at x = -1, a local maximum at x = 0, and a local minimum at x = 1, giving the graph of f a double-well "W" shape. Computing values: f(-1) = 1 - 2 = -1, f(0) = 0, f(1) = 1 - 2 = -1, so the two valleys sit at the same height, which makes sense given the y-axis symmetry. Notice also that f'(-x) = -4x^3 + 4x = -f'(x), so f' is odd, symmetric about the origin, exactly as the differentiation rule predicts for the derivative of an even function.

The second derivative is f''(x) = 12x^2 - 4, an even function (matching the rule again, since differentiating the odd f' should give back an even function), with roots at x = ±1/√3, approximately ±0.577. This is a simple upward-opening parabola, the least complicated of the three shapes, consistent with it sitting furthest down the differentiation chain. Its zeros mark where f' has its own local extrema: f'(x) = 4x^3 - 4x has local turning points exactly at x = ±1/√3, and those same x-values are the inflection points of f, where the double well's sides switch from concave down (near the central hump) to concave up (out toward each valley). Every one of these features cross-checks: f's three horizontal tangents at x = -1, 0, 1 match f''s three zero crossings; f's two inflection points at x = ±1/√3 match f''s two zero crossings; f is the most complex-looking curve (a quartic with two valleys and a hump), f'' is the simplest (a plain parabola), and f is even while f' is odd while f'' is even again, alternating exactly as the symmetry rule predicts.
